title: Policy optimization can be memory-efficient: LLM Alignment Through Successive Policy Re-weighting (SPR)

contributions.purpose: Reduce the compute/memory cost of RL-based policy optimization for LLM alignment down to the level of supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while still leveraging an explicit reward model and online data (unlike DPO), since standard RLHF/PPO must load four models simultaneously.
contributions.mechanism: Successive Policy Re-weighting (SPR): reformulate the TRPO/PPO objective as a constrained optimization solved by a successive minimization algorithm that alternately fits a Q-value function and a log-sum-exp reference (value) function, then updates the policy via a supervised re-weighting loss (increase/decrease log-likelihood of continuations by their advantage Q - W). Only one model is loaded per update step; a sentence-level (horizon=1) simplification (Algorithm 2) reduces Q to the reward r.
contributions.evaluation: Estimated memory (Pythia-1B, TL;DR, batch 2, single device): SPR matches SFT peak memory, well below PPO (four models) and DPO (policy + frozen reference). Only one model loaded per step.
contributions.domain: LLM alignment / reinforcement learning from human feedback
contributions.source_quote: We propose a novel iterative Successive Policy Re-weighting method (SPR, Algorithm 1). SPR utilizes an explicit reward to learn the Q-value function and the log-sum-exp value function, then learns the policy through re-weighting the policy probability based on the Q-value function. SPR only loads one (value or policy) model at every step, achieving policy optimization with the same memory consumption as standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT)

contributions.purpose: Empirically verify that SPR aligns LLMs at least as well as memory-heavier baselines while leveraging offline+online data.
contributions.mechanism: Compare SPR against PPO, DPO, and Best-of-N on a 1B model (Pythia-1B on TL;DR summarization, evaluated by a Pythia-6.9B reward model and GPT-3.5-judged win rate vs reference) and an 8B model (LLaMA3-SFT, OpenLLM leaderboard).
contributions.evaluation: 1B TL;DR: SPR and Best-of-N both beat DPO on reward score; SPR also beats DPO on win rate (Best-of-N does not consistently). 8B OpenLLM leaderboard: SPR beats DPO by 0.22% avg at N=16 and 0.77% at N=3; ~6% improvement on GSM8K; average score progresses 68.66% -> 70.65% over 7 iterations (N=32).
contributions.source_quote: We conduct extensive numerical experiments to verify the effectiveness of the proposed method. Specifically, we compare the SPR with standard PPO and DPO, as well as a Best-of-N algorithm (Dong et al., 2023) on both 1b and 8b models... All our results show the superior performance of the proposed method over standard baselines.

self_declared_provenance.quote: The proposed framework is developed from carefully examining the objective of TRPO/PPO and considers a constrained optimization reformulation from the original problem. A successive minimization algorithm is then proposed to iteratively optimize for the value function and the policy.
methods like online DPO (Dong et al., 2024) and Reinforced Self-Training (ReST, see Gulcehre et al. (2023)) utilize new samples with higher rewards from current model for further policy improvements.

notes: Explicit trade-off / negative acknowledgement in the conclusion: 'The computational time of the proposed method is in general higher than SFT or DPO, and the performance is largely dependent on the number of samples N to estimate the reference function.' So SPR trades wall-clock time and an N-sample budget for its memory savings. Also the 8B leaderboard gains over DPO are small (0.22-0.77% average). Paper was rejected. Win-rate for all methods converges to a stationary level even as reward keeps rising.
